power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Wisdom is a personality trait composed of self-reflection, pro-social behaviors, emotional regulation, acceptance of divergent perspectives, decisiveness, social advising, and spirituality.
Greater levels of wisdom are linked to better overall health, well-being, happiness, life satisfaction, and resilience.
However, the underlying genetic architecture of wisdom remains unexplored.
We assessed wisdom using responses to the SD-WISE-7 in 153,384 23andMe research-consented participants and conducted a multi-ancestry GWAS.
We identified one genome-wide significant locus (rs2325631, p=1.41E-08) near MANEA on chromosome 6.

Wisdom was heritable (h 2 SNP=0.03±4.50E-03) and genetically correlated with numerous traits, including greater subjective well-being, openness, and risk tolerance, and lower neuroticism and loneliness.
Crucially, wisdom was genetically distinct from intelligence and the cognitive component of educational attainment.
Wisdom polygenic scores were associated with psychosocial outcomes, but not cognitive performance in All of Us.
This study advances our understanding of wisdom as a heritable trait that could guide interventions to improve human health.

Wisdom is a personality trait, which has been broadly defined as a multidimensional integration of cognitive insight, self-reflection, and prosocial behavior (such as empathy and compassion) 1 , and is a correlate of health and well-being 2 .

text.text: Wisdom is distinct from intelligence 3, 4 , which broadly involves reasoning, abstraction, problem-solving, and learning from experience 5.

text.text: Among the most widely used instruments for assessing wisdom are the 24-item San Diego Wisdom Scale (SD-WISE-24 6 ) and the shorter 7-item version derived from the expanded scale (SD-WISE-7 7 ), which captures 1) Self-Reflection, 2) Pro-Social Behaviors, 3) Emotional Regulation, 4) Acceptance of Divergent Perspectives, 5) Decisiveness, 6) Social Advising, and 7) Spirituality.

text.text: Prior studies have shown that greater levels of wisdom are positively associated with mental and physical health 1, 8, 9 , happiness 10 , life satisfaction 11 , and resilience 9 , and negatively associated with loneliness 12 , depression, and anxiety 9 .

text.text: Components of wisdom also have potential relevance to behavioral symptoms of neuropsychiatric disorders that have disrupted judgment and personality 13 , such as frontotemporal dementia , 14 and autism spectrum disorder 15.

text.text: Longitudinal studies show that wisdom increases with age 16, 17 and is potentially modifiable, with behavioral intervention studies reporting increases in wisdom or specific wisdom components 18- 20 .

text.text: This suggests wisdom's potential application to interventions that improve health outcomes.
The biological underpinnings of wisdom have been previously theorized 2, 13 .

text.text: The evolutionary Grandmother Hypothesis proposes that post-reproductive adults benefit their kin by investing effort into grandchildren, allowing their children to reproduce sooner 21 .

text.text: Several authors have extended this idea to wisdom, proposing that knowledge and wisdom accumulated through experience likewise allow older adults to benefit their kin 2, 22, 23 .

text.text: However, the genetic underpinnings of wisdom have not been studied, despite other related traits being heritable, such as subjective well-being 24 , resilience 25 , loneliness 26 , and Big Five personality traits Big Five personality traits (i.e., extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness to experience) 27 .

text.text: Elucidating the genetic underpinnings of wisdom can therefore help our understanding of the biological basis of wisdom, enhance diagnostic mechanisms and develop biologically-informed interventions to increase wisdom.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) offer a powerful way to identify the genetic basis of wisdom and its relationships with health, as has been done for other personality and behavioral traits [26] [27] [28] [29] .

text.text: We collected SD-WISE-7 data from a large cohort of genotyped researchconsented participants (N = 161,775) from the 23andMe Research Institute.
Our objectives were four-fold.
First, we examined phenotypic correlations between wisdom and demographic, socioeconomic status (SES), behavioral, psychiatric, and physical health measures.
Second, we performed the first GWAS of wisdom, and calculated its heritability.

Third, using Linkage Disequilibrium Score Regression (LDSC), we estimated genetic correlations between wisdom and a broad range of demographic/socioeconomic, behavioral and personality, externalizing and risk-behavior, psychiatric, physical health, neuroimaging, and cognitive traits from publicly available GWAS.
We also estimated genetic correlations with intelligence, which is conceptually related to but distinct from wisdom 3 .
text.formatted: We also estimated genetic correlations with intelligence, which is conceptually related to but distinct from wisdom <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">3</ref> .

text.text: Fourth, we calculated polygenic scores (PGS) in the All of Us Research Program (AoU) to test the association between genetic liability of wisdom and measures of mental health, psychosocial and physical outcomes, well-being, as well as taskbased cognitive performance.

By integrating psychometric data with large-scale genomic analysis, this study advances our understanding of wisdom as a biologically grounded trait and clarifies its genetic relationship to personality, psychopathology, well-being, and cognition.

text.text: Wisdom was genetically correlated with 3 out of the 6 demographic/SES indicator items tested.

Consistent with SES phenotypic correlations, wisdom was positively genetically correlated with educational attainment (rg = 0.23 ± 0.04, p = 1.52E-08) and its non-cognitive component (NonCog EA; rg = 0.35 ± 0.05, p = 1.72E-13), and household income (rg = 0.27 ± 0.10, p = 6.20E-03), but not the Townsend Deprivation Index (rg = -0.03 ± 0.06, p = 0.69).
Wisdom was not genetically correlated with longevity (rg = -0.17 ± 0.12, p = 0.16) or parental lifespan (rg = 0.02 ± 0.08, p = 0.77).
Wisdom was genetically correlated with 5 of the 6 tested personality traits.

Among these were positive genetic correlations with the Big Five traits, namely extraversion (rg = 0.44 ± 0.07, p = 1.12E-10), openness (rg = 0.41 ± 0.08, p = 1.37E-07), conscientiousness (rg = 0.40 ± 0.07, p = 5.85E-08), and agreeableness (rg = 0.26 ± 0.09, p = 4.90E-03).
Only one Big Five trait, neuroticism, was negatively genetically correlated with wisdom (rg = -0.38 ± 0.05, p = 1.87E-16).
Wisdom was genetically correlated with 7 of the 15 externalizing and impulsivity traits tested.

Total wisdom score was positively genetically correlated with general risk tolerance (rg = 0.36 ± 0.06, p = 6.94E-11), sensation seeking (rg = 0.36 ± 0.07, p = 5.22E-07), and cannabis lifetime use (rg = 0.26 ± 0.07, p = 5.90E-05), which was broadly consistent with phenotypic correlations.

Negative genetic correlations included a subset of impulsivity dimensions: attentional impulsivity (r g = -0.53 ± 0.08, p = 1.89E-10), nonplanning impulsivity (r g = -0.34 ± 0.07, p = 9.02E-07), negative urgency (rg = -0.50 ± 0.10, p = 3.03E-07), and positive urgency (rg = -0.29 ± 0.10, p = 4.50E-03).

Inconsistent with phenotypic correlations, wisdom was not genetically correlated with AUDIT-C (rg = 0.08 ± 0.06, p = 0.20), motor impulsivity (rg = -0.01 ± 0.08, p = 0.90), premeditation (rg = -0.12 ± 0.08, p = 0.16), perseverance (rg = -0.19 ± 0.10, p = 0.07), or with delay discounting after FDR correction (rg = -0.14 ± 0.07, p = 0.04).
None of the 4 neurological conditions tested were genetically correlated with total wisdom score (rg-range = -0.06 ± 0.11 to 0.10 ± 0.05, prange = 0.06 to 0.79).
(ADHD, rg = 0.10 ± 0.05, p = 0.06; autism spectrum disorder, rg = 0.08 ± 0.13, p = 0.53; Alzheimer's, rg = -0.06 ± 0.11, p = 0.58; insomnia, rg = -0.02 ± 0.06, p = 0.79).
Six out of 18 psychiatric disorders were genetically correlated with total wisdom score.

Consistent with phenotypic correlations, wisdom was negatively genetically correlated with major depressive disorder (rg = -0.12 ± 0.04, p = 1.40E-03), and self-reported loneliness (rg = -0.27 ± 0.06, p = 8.45E-07).

Wisdom scores were also positively genetically correlated with cannabis use disorder (rg = 0.24 ± 0.08, p = 3.80E-03), self-reported well-being (rg = 0.34 ± 0.06, p = 1.52E-09), bipolar disorder (rg = 0.19 ± 0.06, p = 5.00E-04), and schizophrenia (rg = 0.22 ± 0.04, p = 6.95E-08).

text.text: This is the first study to explore the genetic basis of wisdom.
We collected SD-WISE-7 responses at scale (N = 153,384) in 23andMe research participants for whom genome-wide genotype data were already available.
We found that wisdom was heritable (h 2 SNP = 0.03), in alignment with other dispositional traits (e.g., 24, 27, 49 ).
text.formatted: We found that wisdom was heritable (h 2 SNP = 0.03), in alignment with other dispositional traits (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">49</ref> ).

text.text: We identified one genome-wide significant locus, led by the intergenic variant rs2325631 near MANEA, and gene-and transcriptome-based analyses converged on ADK.
Wisdom scores were associated with better health and well-being at phenotypic (within cohort) and genetic (with external cohorts) levels, supporting phenotypic findings by others 2, 9 .
text.formatted: Wisdom scores were associated with better health and well-being at phenotypic (within cohort) and genetic (with external cohorts) levels, supporting phenotypic findings by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> .

text.text: Our genetic correlations were strongest with education and personality traits and not cognition.

Wisdom PGS analysis similarly revealed positive associations with broad wellbeing outcomes that were partially attenuated by PGS of personality and non-cognitive educational attainment but not by cognitive performance.

Together, our findings support a biological basis of wisdom and relationships with health and well-being that may be partially mediated by pleiotropy with personality traits that promote healthy lifestyles.

Wisdom is defined as a multifaceted personality trait with longstanding roots in spirituality that is composed of good decision-making abilities, flexible and reflective thinking, prosociality, emotional regulation, and the application of knowledge beyond cognitive ability 23 .

text.text: SD-WISE-7 was developed to capture these characteristics 7 .

text.text: Consistently, we found that wisdom was genetically correlated with other personality traits (e.g., the Big Five), but not at unity, emphasizing that wisdom is a distinct personality trait that is fundamental to human experiences.

We observed phenotypic and genetic associations between wisdom and numerous measures of physical and mental health, consistent with other personality traits (e.g., extraversion, openness, compassion, among others) 24, 27, [50] [51] [52] [53] [54] [55] [56] .

text.text: Wisdom and its components (e.g., Pro-Social Behaviors, Emotional Regulation, and Social Advising) are malleable across the lifespan 18, 19, [57] [58] [59] [60] , suggesting that wisdom may hold promise as a target for psychosocial and behavioral interventions to improve overall well-being 4 , as it has been explored for other personality traits 61.

text.text: While we focused on total wisdom scores, divergences across the subcomponents indicate there is value to studying them individually.

For example, although total wisdom scores were phenotypically correlated with affective measures, the items of Decisiveness ("I tend to postpone making major decisions as long as I can") and Emotional Regulation (e.g., "I remain calm under pressure") drove these associations.
This is consistent with a prior SD-WISE study 9 , suggesting that Emotional Regulation may be a critical channel through which wisdom genetically relates to health.
text.formatted: This is consistent with a prior SD-WISE study <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">9</ref> , suggesting that Emotional Regulation may be a critical channel through which wisdom genetically relates to health.

text.text: In addition, only examining total wisdom scores may occlude some associations.

For example, older age showed strong but opposing item-level relationships (e.g., positive with Decisiveness, negative with Acceptance of Divergent Perspectives) that were masked by overall positive associations with total wisdom scores.
Whether these item-specific patterns extend to genetic correlations remains unknown, as item-level GWAS data were unavailable.
Some conceptions of wisdom include intelligence, reasoning, and knowledge among its components 62 .
text.formatted: Some conceptions of wisdom include intelligence, reasoning, and knowledge among its components <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">62</ref> .

text.text: Modern psychosocial frameworks and study measures, however, conceptualize wisdom as distinct from intelligence 3, 63 .

text.text: In particular for SD-WISE, wisdom scores are dissociable from fluid intelligence, executive function, and processing speed 4 .
text.formatted: In particular for SD-WISE, wisdom scores are dissociable from fluid intelligence, executive function, and processing speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">4</ref> .

text.text: This is consistent with our findings that wisdom scores are genetically uncorrelated with intelligence/cognitive function, executive function, and cognitive performance, and wisdom PGS associations were unaltered when modelled alongside cognitive performance PGS.

Wisdom PGS also did not associate with the four cognitive tasks collected in All of Us participants, despite expectations that some tasks (e.g., emotional recognition) would reflect SD-WISE-7 item responses.

While this may suggest no associations between wisdom score and broad cognitive function, another study has identified modest positive associations between performance-based wisdom measures and crystallized intelligence 64 .

text.text: We cannot rule out wisdom associations with cognition could be overlooked by our use of the SD-WISE-7 self-report and/or relatively small target samples.
Despite the lack of associations with cognition, wisdom was phenotypically and genetically correlated with educational attainment.
Many factors outside of cognitive ability contribute to educational attainment, including socioeconomic circumstance 65 and personality 66, 67 .

text.text: We found that the non-cognitive genetic component of educational attainment (NonCogEA) 68 was genetically correlated with total wisdom scores, and wisdom PGS associations were attenuated when modeled jointly with NonCogEA PGS, suggesting substantial shared genetic influences between the two traits.

text.text: We suggest that wisdom's genetic relationship with educational attainment is sustained by non-cognitive factors (e.g., personality, SES) that support higher achievement, rather than with cognitive ability.
Overall, we find that wisdom phenotypically and genetically associates with better physical and mental health, consistent with prior phenotypic observations 1, 7, 9 .

text.text: This pattern was concentrated in psychiatric rather than physical health, though we tested far fewer physical health traits.
Perhaps surprisingly, wisdom was not genetically correlated with parental lifespan or longevity, despite the theory that wisdom accrued over life promotes post-reproductive inclusive fitness 22, 23 .
text.formatted: Perhaps surprisingly, wisdom was not genetically correlated with parental lifespan or longevity, despite the theory that wisdom accrued over life promotes post-reproductive inclusive fitness <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">23</ref> .

text.text: Instead, we found that wisdom PGS were most strongly associated with self-reported measures of social satisfaction and mental health, compared to psychiatric diagnosis from electronic health records, suggesting that wisdom's genetic signal tracks broader psychosocial outcomes.
While we generally found favorable wisdom associations with health, we report some unexpected genetic relationships with schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and cannabis use traits.
Total wisdom scores were negatively phenotypically correlated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, whereas genetic correlations were positive.

Furthermore, although we had no phenotypic measures for cannabis use, genetic correlations with lifetime cannabis use and cannabis use disorder were also positive despite finding no other genetic correlations with substance use.

This is not unprecedented: favourable genetic relationships between schizophrenia and educational attainment 69 , or alcohol use and psychiatric conditions 70 , were explained by their shared genetic liability with other unaccounted for traits (e.g., SES).

text.text: Likewise, other personality traits (e.g., openness, extraversion), which also show similar paradoxical positive genetic correlations with schizophrenia and cannabis use, may mediate the inconsistent observations in our study (Supplementary Figure 6).

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, total wisdom scores were quantified through subjective self-reported items.

SD-WISE-7 is the most feasible wisdom measure to use at the scale required for GWAS 7 , using structural equation modeling to weight each of the SD-WISE-7 items (rather than using a sum of the scores) may better fit our data (Supplementary Figure 11).
text.formatted: SD-WISE-7 is the most feasible wisdom measure to use at the scale required for GWAS <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">7</ref> , using structural equation modeling to weight each of the SD-WISE-7 items (rather than using a sum of the scores) may better fit our data (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">11</ref>).

text.text: Furthermore, wisdom could be defined in other ways, including with other questionnaires, which might yield different results than those presented here.
Second, while social desirability may influence participant self-reports, one previous study found a low correlation between SD-WISE responding and social desirability 6 .
text.formatted: Second, while social desirability may influence participant self-reports, one previous study found a low correlation between SD-WISE responding and social desirability <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">6</ref> .

text.text: Third, wisdom measures were collected as part of a larger study including individuals who all reported using opioids in their lifetime, which could have biased our observations.
However, we did not find any evidence that opioid use was genetically correlated with total wisdom scores.
Fourth, given the absence of clear functional evidence linking the MANEA locus to wisdom and the pleiotropic associations of ADK (e.g., 41, 45 ), both findings require replication.
text.formatted: Fourth, given the absence of clear functional evidence linking the MANEA locus to wisdom and the pleiotropic associations of ADK (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">41,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">45</ref> ), both findings require replication.

text.text: Fifth, our analyses were all cross-sectional and underpowered to study the direction or causality of wisdom relationships.

Finally, only the European-like ancestry GWAS was well-powered to detect specific associations, which may be particularly relevant to wisdom given there are known cross-cultural differences in wisdom perception 71.

text.text: Overall, we present the first evidence that wisdom is a heritable trait with genetic links to personality, behavior, and health, but not cognition.

Our results show that greater genetic liability to wisdom is associated with a constellation of health-related outcomes that are only partially 454 attributable to the genetics of other personality dimensions.

As a biologically-grounded yet 455 environmentally malleable trait, future investigations with better powered genetic data may 456 provide additional support for wisdom as a valuable target to broadly improve well-being.

text.text: Participants rated items on a five-point Likert scale with responses including "Strongly disagree", "Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree", and "Strongly agree".
Responses were scored 0-4; the four negatively worded items were reverse coded (denoted below as "R").
Total wisdom scores were the sum of all seven items and ranged 0 -28.
Complete responses to all seven items were required.
The 7 survey items were: 1) Emotional Regulation: I remain calm under pressure.
3) Acceptance of Divergent Perspectives: I enjoy being exposed to diverse viewpoints.
4) Decisiveness: I tend to postpone making major decisions as long as I can (R).

Phenotypic correlations (rp) of total wisdom scores and individual SD-WISE-7 items with 31 demographic, health-related behavioral measures, and psychiatric phenotypes were calculated in up to 161,775 research participants with complete data available.
We calculated unadjusted Pearson correlations and partial correlations that were adjusted for age, sex, education, and household income.
Multiple testing was accounted for by applying a FDR correction across the 31 tests in each model.
See Supplementary Materials for additional details.
Ancestry-specific GWAS included 131,870 European-like, 16,812 Latin American-like, and 4,702 African-like unrelated participants.
Ancestry was determined through an analysis of local ancestry (Supplementary Materials).
